Random Effects Meta-Analysis of Generic Effect Sizes

Source: R/meta_es.R
meta_es.Rd

Pools independent effect sizes given their sampling variances: the general engine behind meta_smd and meta_r, exposed for any effect metric whose estimates are approximately normal with known variances. The random effects model is the default and the fit reports the full uncertainty picture in one table: the pooled estimate with its confidence interval, the between-study standard deviation tau, the between-study variance tau-squared with its Q-profile confidence interval, I-squared with an interval mapped from the tau-squared limits, H-squared, Cochran's Q test, and, always, a prediction interval for the effect in a new study. Reporting the prediction interval by default is deliberate: when heterogeneity is real, the confidence interval for the average effect understates what the next study will show, and the package treats “where will the next study land” as part of the answer, not an option.

Usage

meta_es(
  yi,
  vi,
  method = c("reml", "pm", "dl", "fe"),
  hartung_knapp = TRUE,
  conf_level = 0.95
)

Arguments

yi

Numeric vector of effect sizes, one per independent study.

vi

Sampling variances of yi, one per study.

method

Between-study variance estimator: "reml" (restricted maximum likelihood, the default), "pm" (Paule-Mandel), "dl" (DerSimonian-Laird), or "fe" (a fixed effect / common effect analysis, which assumes tau-squared is zero and reports no prediction interval).

hartung_knapp

Logical: apply the Hartung-Knapp-Sidik-Jonkman small-sample adjustment (the pooled standard error rescaled from the weighted residuals, with a t reference on \(k - 1\) degrees of freedom)? Default TRUE. The adjusted standard error is not bounded below by the conventional one, so the interval can be narrower than the normal interval; see The Hartung-Knapp adjustment and When q is small in Details. Identical effect sizes give a zero adjusted standard error and a warning; see Identical effect sizes. Ignored for method = "fe".

conf_level

Confidence level for all intervals. Defaults to 0.95.

Value

A data.frame (class dmar_meta, a dmar_tbl) with rows estimate, se, test_statistic (the estimate divided by se), p_value, ci_lower / ci_upper, prediction_lower / prediction_upper, tau2 with tau2_ci_lower / tau2_ci_upper, tau, I2 with limits, H2, Q / Q_df / Q_p, and n_studies (the number of studies, \(k\)). The estimator and adjustment are recorded in the "method" and "hartung_knapp" attributes. The reference distribution of test_statistic and p_value depends on the adjustment, and the attributes test_distribution and test_df record it: "t" on \(k - 1\) degrees of freedom under the Hartung-Knapp adjustment, "normal" (with test_df NA) without it, as the line under the printed table says. The attributes hartung_knapp_q (the weighted residual mean square \(q\)) and se_conventional are recorded whenever the adjustment is applied. When the effect sizes are identical and the Hartung-Knapp adjustment is applied, se is zero, the limits equal the estimate, and the function warns (see Identical effect sizes in Details).

Details

The model is \(y_i = \mu + u_i + e_i\) with \(u_i \sim N(0, \tau^2)\) and \(e_i \sim N(0, v_i)\), \(v_i\) treated as known. The \(\tau^2\) confidence interval inverts the generalized Q statistic (Viechtbauer, 2007); the I-squared interval maps the \(\tau^2\) interval through the typical within-study variance of Higgins and Thompson (2002). The prediction interval follows Higgins, Thompson, and Spiegelhalter (2009), using t with \(k - 2\) degrees of freedom, and requires at least three studies.

The Hartung-Knapp adjustment. With weights \(w_i = 1/(v_i + \hat{\tau}^2)\) and pooled estimate \(\hat{\mu}\), the adjusted standard error is the conventional one, \((\sum w_i)^{-1/2}\), multiplied by \(\sqrt{q}\), where $$q = \frac{1}{k - 1} \sum_{i=1}^{k} w_i (y_i - \hat{\mu})^2$$ is the weighted residual mean square on \(k - 1\) degrees of freedom (Röver, Knapp, & Friede, 2015), and the interval is the pooled estimate plus and minus the \(1 - \alpha/2\) quantile of the t distribution on \(k - 1\) degrees of freedom times that standard error. The function applies this, the unmodified method, as test = "knha" in metafor does: \(q\) is not replaced by \(\max(1, q)\). With few studies the coverage of the adjusted interval is closer to the nominal level than that of the normal interval. The prediction interval uses the standard error of the pooled estimate that the confidence interval uses, so under the adjustment it narrows and widens with \(q\) as well.

When q is small. Because \(q\) is not replaced by \(\max(1, q)\), the adjusted standard error is smaller than the conventional one whenever \(q\) is below 1, which is common (when the effects are homogeneous, in most samples). That alone does not make the interval narrower than the normal interval, since the adjusted interval uses a t quantile on \(k - 1\) degrees of freedom: it is narrower exactly when \(q\) is below the squared ratio of the normal quantile to the t quantile, which for a 95 percent interval is 0.02, 0.21, 0.50, and 0.75 at \(k\) = 2, 3, 5, and 10. A small \(q\) is part of the reference distribution of the method and not a fault in the data: when the weights are the true ones, the pooled estimate minus the mean effect, divided by the adjusted standard error, follows the t distribution exactly, small values of \(q\) included. Röver, Knapp, and Friede (2015) describe the modification \(\max(1, q)\), which never gives a standard error below the conventional one; it is not applied here. In the simulations run for this function the unmodified interval was at or near the nominal level when the effects were homogeneous or the studies equally precise, and below it (0.86 to 0.89 for a nominal 0.95, with the normal interval at 0.70 to 0.87) when one study was far more precise than the rest and the effects were heterogeneous. When the adjusted interval is much narrower than the conventional one, report both; hartung_knapp = FALSE gives the second. The attributes hartung_knapp_q and se_conventional hold \(q\) and the conventional standard error for that comparison. No warning is given for a \(q\) between 0 and 1, which is the method working as defined.

Identical effect sizes. When every effect size is the same, exactly or up to rounding error, \(q\) is 0 and so is the adjusted standard error. The confidence interval and the prediction interval then have no width, and the t statistic is infinite, or undefined when the common effect size is zero. That is the arithmetic of the method at its boundary and not evidence of an effect known exactly: each effect size still has its sampling variance, and identical values arise from coarse rounding, from one study entered more than once, or by chance with two or three studies. The function reports the numbers as computed, as test = "knha" in metafor does, and warns with a condition of class dmar_meta_hk_zero_se that states the conventional standard error and interval. The condition carries the number of studies as n_studies, the pooled estimate as estimate, the conventional standard error as se_conventional, and the limits of the normal interval that standard error gives as lower_conventional and upper_conventional. For four effect sizes of 0.5 with sampling variances of 0.04, the adjusted limits are 0.5 and 0.5; the conventional standard error is 0.1 and the normal interval 0.304 to 0.696. The check is made on the effect sizes themselves: effect sizes that differ in any digit beyond rounding error (0.5 against \(0.5 + 10^{-9}\)) are not identical, give a small positive \(q\), and raise no warning.

I-squared is reported because readers expect it, but note its well-known limitation: it is a proportion of variability, not an amount, so the same tau matched with larger studies yields a larger I-squared. The quantity with direct scientific meaning is tau (the between-study standard deviation, in the metric of yi) together with the prediction interval.

References

DerSimonian, R., & Laird, N. (1986). Meta-analysis in clinical trials. Controlled Clinical Trials, 7(3), 177–188.

Hartung, J., & Knapp, G. (2001). On tests of the overall treatment effect in meta-analysis with normally distributed responses. Statistics in Medicine, 20(12), 1771–1782. doi:10.1002/sim.791

Higgins, J. P. T., & Thompson, S. G. (2002). Quantifying heterogeneity in a meta-analysis. Statistics in Medicine, 21(11), 1539–1558. doi:10.1002/sim.1186

Higgins, J. P. T., Thompson, S. G., & Spiegelhalter, D. J. (2009). A re-evaluation of random-effects meta-analysis. Journal of the Royal Statistical Society: Series A, 172(1), 137–159. doi:10.1111/j.1467-985X.2008.00552.x

Raudenbush, S. W. (1984). Magnitude of teacher expectancy effects on pupil IQ as a function of the credibility of expectancy induction: A synthesis of findings from 18 experiments. Journal of Educational Psychology, 76(1), 85–97.

Röver, C., Knapp, G., & Friede, T. (2015). Hartung-Knapp-Sidik-Jonkman approach and its modification for random-effects meta-analysis with few studies. BMC Medical Research Methodology, 15, Article 99. doi:10.1186/s12874-015-0091-1

Viechtbauer, W. (2007). Confidence intervals for the amount of heterogeneity in meta-analysis. Statistics in Medicine, 26(1), 37–52. doi:10.1002/sim.2514

See also

meta_smd and meta_r for the metric- specific front ends; meta_contrast for focused moderator contrasts; combine_p for combined significance tests; plot_forest to see the studies and the pool together.

Other meta-analysis: combine_p(), meta_contrast(), meta_r(), meta_smd(), plot_forest()

Author

Ken Kelley kkelley@nd.edu

Examples

# The teacher expectancy studies (Raudenbush, 1984), pooled in the d
# metric with variances from the standard large-sample formula.
data(teacher_expectancy)
d <- teacher_expectancy$d
n_e <- teacher_expectancy$n_experimental
n_c <- teacher_expectancy$n_control
v <- (n_e + n_c) / (n_e * n_c) + d^2 / (2 * (n_e + n_c))
meta_es(d, v)
#>  term             value 
#>  estimate         0.055 
#>  se               0.036 
#>  test_statistic   1.544 
#>  p_value          0.1401
#>  ci_lower         -0.020
#>  ci_upper         0.130 
#>  prediction_lower -0.020
#>  prediction_upper 0.130 
#>  tau2             0.000 
#>  tau2_ci_lower    0.000 
#>  tau2_ci_upper    0.051 
#>  tau              0.000 
#>  I2               0.000 
#>  I2_ci_lower      0.000 
#>  I2_ci_upper      66.144
#>  H2               1.000 
#>  Q                17.067
#>  Q_df             18    
#>  Q_p              0.5185
#>  n_studies        19    
#> 
#> Confidence level: 95%
#> 
#> test_statistic: referred to Student's t on 18 df (Hartung-Knapp adjustment)

# A fixed effect (common effect) analysis of the same studies.
meta_es(d, v, method = "fe")
#>  term             value 
#>  estimate         0.055 
#>  se               0.037 
#>  test_statistic   1.503 
#>  p_value          0.1328
#>  ci_lower         -0.017
#>  ci_upper         0.127 
#>  prediction_lower <NA>  
#>  prediction_upper <NA>  
#>  tau2             0.000 
#>  tau2_ci_lower    <NA>  
#>  tau2_ci_upper    <NA>  
#>  tau              0.000 
#>  I2               0.000 
#>  I2_ci_lower      <NA>  
#>  I2_ci_upper      <NA>  
#>  H2               1.000 
#>  Q                17.067
#>  Q_df             18    
#>  Q_p              0.5185
#>  n_studies        19    
#> 
#> Confidence level: 95%
#> 
#> test_statistic: referred to the standard normal

# The adjusted standard error beside the conventional one. Five effect
# sizes that agree closely give a weighted residual mean square q far
# below 1, so the adjusted standard error is a small fraction of the
# conventional one; both intervals are worth reporting.
close <- meta_es(c(.30, .32, .29, .31, .33), c(.04, .05, .03, .06, .04))
attr(close, "hartung_knapp_q")
#> [1] 0.006860532
attr(close, "se_conventional")
#> [1] 0.09128709
meta_es(c(.30, .32, .29, .31, .33), c(.04, .05, .03, .06, .04),
        hartung_knapp = FALSE)
#>  term             value 
#>  estimate         0.308 
#>  se               0.091 
#>  test_statistic   3.376 
#>  p_value          0.0007
#>  ci_lower         0.129 
#>  ci_upper         0.487 
#>  prediction_lower 0.018 
#>  prediction_upper 0.599 
#>  tau2             0.000 
#>  tau2_ci_lower    0.000 
#>  tau2_ci_upper    0.000 
#>  tau              0.000 
#>  I2               0.000 
#>  I2_ci_lower      0.000 
#>  I2_ci_upper      0.000 
#>  H2               1.000 
#>  Q                0.027 
#>  Q_df             4
